snippet.title: How to become 37.78 times better at anything | Atomic Habits summary (by James Clear)
snippet.description:
Atomic Habits can help you improve every day, no matter what your goals are. As one of the world's leading experts on habit formation, James Clear reveals practical strategies that will help you form good habits, break bad ones, and master tiny behaviors that lead to big changes.

If you're having trouble changing your habits, the problem isn't you. Instead, the issue is with your system. There is a reason bad habits repeat themselves over and over again, it's not that you are not willing to change, but that you have the wrong system for changing.
 
“You do not rise to the level of your goals. You fall to the level of your systems” - James Clear 

I’m a huge fan of this book, and as soon as I read it I knew it was going to make a big difference in my life, so I couldn’t wait to make a video on this book and share my ideas.

Here is a link to James Clear’s website, where I found he uploads a tonne of useful posts on motivation, habit formation and human psychology.

https://jamesclear.com/


If you liked this summary and you want to go deeper into Atomic Habits, here is a link to the book (Nothing Beats the book!)

📕Atomic Habits by James Clear - https://amzn.to/2Yk6ulK

If you are more into Audiobooks, here is a link to that. You can get this audiobook for free if you sign up for a free Audible trial with the link below. 

🎧Grab Atomic Habits audiobook on an Audible trial with 2 free books - https://amzn.to/3A5r32l


🗎If you want to help out my channel, please consider grabbing the PDF mindmap and illustrations I made to go along with this summary - https://escapingordinary.gumroad.com/

Lessons you will learn from reading Atomic Habits
  •  How to make time for new habits ;
  •  How to overcome a lack of motivation and willpower;
  •  How to design your environment to make success easier;
  •  How to get back on track if your habits break down
  •  How to overcome the plateau of latent potential

I found Seth Godin’s books while I was in college, and I quoted them throughout MBA school and law school. I absolutely fell in love with his approach to marketing. I’ve read (and listened to) all his books multiple times, and I own them on every format.

- This is Marketing

snippet.title: A CHRISTMAS CAROL BY CHARLES DICKENS - ANIMATED BOOK SUMMARY
snippet.description:
Check out my website: https://schraderacademy.io/

A Christmas Carol, is almost certainly the most famous and most widely read of all of Charles Dickens’s stories. At just under 28,500 words, it is a novella rather than a novel; by comparison, the equally famous Gone with the Wind is well over 400,000 words.
 Yet this very short book, with its moving message of forgiveness and redemption, is one of the most popular in the world. It has never been out of print since it was first published in London in 1843 and has been translated into many languages.
 As with other Dickens stories, A Christmas Carol called attention to the plight of the desperately poor in London – especially the children. It also had an influence on the way people in Britain and the United States celebrated Christmas, right down to the present day.
 This short book consists of five chapters, which at the time were called “staves.”
 Stave One: The story opens in London on Christmas Eve, seven years to the day after the death of Ebenezer Scrooge’s business partner, Jacob Marley. Scrooge himself is a selfish, bitter old man. His occupation is not clearly stated but he seems to be a moneylender and is extremely punishing when it comes to having his clients pay back their loans.
 When two local merchants ask Scrooge for a donation to help the poor, he refuses to give them anything.
 Scrooge’s bookkeeper, Bob Cratchit, is overworked and rudely treated. Scrooge will not allow him enough coal to keep the office warm in December and only grudgingly gives the man a day off to spend Christmas with his family.
 That night, back at his own empty, dark, depressing home, Scrooge is visited by the ghost of Marley. The ghost has a terrible appearance, wrapped with enormous chains and dragging heavy lockboxes. The ghost of Marley explains that: “I wear the chain I forged in life," replied the Ghost. "I made it link by link, and yard by yard; I girded it on of my own free will, and of my own free will I wore it.”
 Marley tells Scrooge that unless he changes his selfish ways, he too will end up just like Marley. Scrooge refuses to believe him, and so Marley tells him to expect visitations from three spirits before the night is over.
 In Stave two Scrooge awakens to the presence of the Spirit of Christmas Past, a glowing, angelic figure robed in white. The spirit makes him revisit his earlier Christmases, when he was a boy left alone at boarding school over the holiday; a youth apprenticed to his jolly master, Mr. Fezziwig; and, finally, a young man choosing wealth over love when his fiancée, Belle, returns his engagement ring because she believes he loves gold better than he loves her.
 Scrooge is quite distraught by what he has been forced to remember and demands to return to his room alone.
 In Stave 3, Scrooge again awakens to a ghost in his house, this time the Sprit of Christmas Present. He is an enormous and very jovial man who is surrounded by the most wonderful feast imaginable, along with a blazing hearthfire, a Christmas tree, and many gifts.
 The spirt shows Scrooge how others celebrate Christmas, including Scrooge’s kind-hearted nephew, Fred, and Bob Cratchit and his very poor but happy family. 
 We meet Cratchit’s sweet-natured young son, Tiny Tim, who is ill and crippled. The spirit informs Scrooge that if the boy cannot get a doctor’s care – which, of course, his family cannot afford – he will die. 
 The spirit also shows Scrooge two cold, starving, neglected children, and tells him their names are Ignorance and Want for they have no one to care for them. Scrooge asks the ghost: “Have they no refuge or resource”? The spirit replies with Scrooge’s own callous remarks asking: “Are there no workhouses?”
 In Stave four, the final visitor, the Spirit of Christmas Yet to Come, is the most terrifying, for it is a mere specter in black and resembles the Grim Reaper. By now Scrooge has been shaken by all that he has been forced to see and the spirit does not hesitate to take advantage of his vulnerable state.
 Scrooge is shown that at his death, no one mourns for him, and that nearly everyone is simply glad that such cold-hearted man is finally gone. Even worse, he is shown that Tiny Tim has died and the Cratchit family will never be the same.
 Scrooge realizes that his life has served little purpose and, indeed, has only been a source of sorrow and misery to others. When the spirit forces him to look at his own cold and lonely gravestone, Scrooge allows his heart to change at last.
 In Stave five, Scrooge awakens in his room, and it is Christmas morning. Overjoyed at finding that it is not too late for him to change his ways and make a positive difference in the lives of his family, friends, and employees, he first takes gifts and good food to the Cratchit family.

A Christmas Carol, is almost certainly the most famous and most widely read of all of Charles Dickens’s stories. At just under 28,500 words, it is a novella rather than a novel; by comparison, the equally famous Gone with the Wind is well over 400,000 words.
 Yet this very short book, with its moving message of forgiveness and redemption, is one of the most popular in the world. It has never been out of print since it was first published in London in 1843 and has been translated into many languages.
 As with other Dickens stories, A Christmas Carol called attention to the plight of the desperately poor in London – especially the children. It also had an influence on the way people in Britain and the United States celebrated Christmas, right down to the present day.
 This short book consists of five chapters, which at the time were called “staves.”
 Stave One: The story opens in London on Christmas Eve, seven years to the day after the death of Ebenezer Scrooge’s business partner, Jacob Marley. Scrooge himself is a selfish, bitter old man. His occupation is not clearly stated but he seems to be a moneylender and is extremely punishing when it comes to having his clients pay back their loans.
 When two local merchants ask Scrooge for a donation to help the poor, he refuses to give them anything.
 Scrooge’s bookkeeper, Bob Cratchit, is overworked and rudely treated. Scrooge will not allow him enough coal to keep the office warm in December and only grudgingly gives the man a day off to spend Christmas with his family.
 That night, back at his own empty, dark, depressing home, Scrooge is visited by the ghost of Marley. The ghost has a terrible appearance, wrapped with enormous chains and dragging heavy lockboxes. The ghost of Marley explains that: “I wear the chain I forged in life," replied the Ghost. "I made it link by link, and yard by yard; I girded it on of my own free will, and of my own free will I wore it.”
 Marley tells Scrooge that unless he changes his selfish ways, he too will end up just like Marley. Scrooge refuses to believe him, and so Marley tells him to expect visitations from three spirits before the night is over.
 In Stave two Scrooge awakens to the presence of the Spirit of Christmas Past, a glowing, angelic figure robed in white. The spirit makes him revisit his earlier Christmases, when he was a boy left alone at boarding school over the holiday; a youth apprenticed to his jolly master, Mr. Fezziwig; and, finally, a young man choosing wealth over love when his fiancée, Belle, returns his engagement ring because she believes he loves gold better than he loves her.
 Scrooge is quite distraught by what he has been forced to remember and demands to return to his room alone.
 In Stave 3, Scrooge again awakens to a ghost in his house, this time the Sprit of Christmas Present. He is an enormous and very jovial man who is surrounded by the most wonderful feast imaginable, along with a blazing hearthfire, a Christmas tree, and many gifts.
 The spirt shows Scrooge how others celebrate Christmas, including Scrooge’s kind-hearted nephew, Fred, and Bob Cratchit and his very poor but happy family. 
 We meet Cratchit’s sweet-natured young son, Tiny Tim, who is ill and crippled. The spirit informs Scrooge that if the boy cannot get a doctor’s care – which, of course, his family cannot afford – he will die. 
 The spirit also shows Scrooge two cold, starving, neglected children, and tells him their names are Ignorance and Want for they have no one to care for them. Scrooge asks the ghost: “Have they no refuge or resource”? The spirit replies with Scrooge’s own callous remarks asking: “Are there no workhouses?”
 In Stave four, the final visitor, the Spirit of Christmas Yet to Come, is the most terrifying, for it is a mere specter in black and resembles the Grim Reaper. By now Scrooge has been shaken by all that he has been forced to see and the spirit does not hesitate to take advantage of his vulnerable state.
 Scrooge is shown that at his death, no one mourns for him, and that nearly everyone is simply glad that such cold-hearted man is finally gone. Even worse, he is shown that Tiny Tim has died and the Cratchit family will never be the same.
 Scrooge realizes that his life has served little purpose and, indeed, has only been a source of sorrow and misery to others. When the spirit forces him to look at his own cold and lonely gravestone, Scrooge allows his heart to change at last.
 In Stave five, Scrooge awakens in his room, and it is Christmas morning. Overjoyed at finding that it is not too late for him to change his ways and make a positive difference in the lives of his family, friends, and employees, he first takes gifts and good food to the Cratchit family.
